name: The Everyday 20-Something
one_liner: The frictionless majority: buys twice a week on proximity, price and open-now, shrugs at the fusion-vs-traditional debate entirely — and is quietly won over anyway by a brisket that's better than a taco truck has any right to be.
quote: It's right there and it does the job. But the brisket one's actually good — properly good. I didn't expect that from a truck.

items.text: Solve 'I'm hungry' with the least possible effort — fast, filling, and right on the route home or between shifts. BorderBlend wins because it's the easy default, not because it's a destination.
Get full without spending restaurant money. Value is the whole relationship — as long as a couple of items and a drink stays well under the 'is this basically a restaurant now?' line.

Genuinely does not care whether it's fusion or traditional — 'it's tacos' — which is the useful signal: the brand's big strategy debate is invisible to them. What actually moves them is the brisket over-delivering against low expectations.
High-frequency but completely unplanned — a couple of times a week, dictated by shifts and whatever's on the way. 'I don't plan it. It's just on the way.'
Orders the brisket as the one thing worth a small detour; everything else is 'just food.' Low menu curiosity, high loyalty to the single hero item.
Disciplined solo (one item, then finishes eating at home), a pushover in a group — gets swept up and spends more when friends pile on. The group order is where the basket grows.
Downloaded the app once to order ahead, never really used it, maybe deleted it — 'faster to walk up than mess with the phone.'

First contact is human and physical, never brand-owned: sheer proximity to a SkyTrain stop or campus, a festival appearance, and friends saying 'get the brisket one.' 'I found out where they'd be from my friends, not from the brand.'
Will happily watch a good first-bite video if the algorithm serves it, but never follows, seeks out, or posts — a watcher, not a poster. Content reaches them by accident, not by subscription.

If the truck isn't where it usually is, they don't hunt for it — they just get something else. Truck-status uncertainty is experienced as pure, silent churn, and it's the single fastest way to lose them.
Price is creeping from 'a deal' toward 'normal' — the moment they start 'doing the math,' they'd rather sit down somewhere. A soft ceiling (~$15 with a drink) is quietly forming.
On a work break with no time to spare, a line down the block is a dealbreaker — and the app never solved it, so it stayed unused. Beating 'walk up and wait' is the bar order-ahead has to clear.

blocks.title: What would deepen the relationship & drive subscription

items.text: A genuine student discount or a real deal is the only email hook that works — 'tell me how to spend less,' not 'the story of our brisket.' Make it about money and it turns a treat back into a default.

A narrow, utility-only alert — 'we're here today' or 'brisket's half off' — is the one push they'd actually accept, because it answers the is-it-here question and offers value. Anything resembling brand content is a hard no.

Zero-friction loyalty they didn't even know existed — 'phone number at the window, done.' The instant it needs an account, a password, or a download, they're gone; make it effortless and this segment is an easy sell.

Starts transactional and faintly amused by the whole idea of caring about a taco truck ('why would I follow a taco truck?'), then gets quietly, genuinely won over by the brisket — a small 'oh, okay' moment that keeps them coming back.
Low-grade wariness about price is the only thing that could gently lose them — no drama, just a slow drift to 'the place I can sit down.' Entirely winnable back on value and ease.
